question: Does the Lord act independently of the karma of souls?

sides.position: The Lord depends neither on karma nor on the soul; he produces the effect at will, all at once or in sequence.
arguments: Those who desire the fruits of action depend on Maheśvara, not he on them (PABh on PS 2.6).
Karma bears fruit when favoured by the Lord's will and can be fruitless without it, as Yayāti's was; beings act because they depend on his will (SDS ch. 6).
The Lord, whose desires are fulfilled, needs nothing karma produces; effects do not arise at once because his power of action follows his will (SDS ch. 6).

sides.position: The Lord's dispensation depends on beings' karma; otherwise he would be partial and cruel; and a Lord who is merely the efficient cause cannot escape either partiality or circular dependence on karma.
arguments: Partiality and cruelty do not belong to the Lord because he depends [on karma] (BS 2.1.34).

A Lord who makes beings low, middle and high would have passion and aversion; if he depends on karma, Lord and karma depend on each other, and beginninglessness does not remove the fault (Śaṅkara on BS 2.2.37).

sides.position: The Lord is the cause who makes human effort fruitful; results do not arise without human action (Nyāya Sūtra 4.1.19-21 as read by its commentators).
arguments: Human action is sometimes seen to be fruitless, so the Lord is a cause; yet without human action there is no fruit; the objection fails because the result is brought about by him.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Pāśupatas deny that the Lord depends on karma; Vedānta holds that denying dependence makes him partial.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Pāśupata speaks from the divine standpoint (the Lord's freedom), Vedānta and Nyāya from the causal standpoint (karma's regularity); the SDS reply itself gives karma a fruit-bearing role under the Lord's will.
P1-level: at the conventional level karma governs results; the Lord's freedom concerns the level of the ultimate cause.
No reconciliation: the traditions disagree about whether the Lord could act otherwise than karma requires.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Pāśupata tradition explicitly denies that the Lord is karma-dependent (PABh 2.6); Śaṅkara explicitly argues that a karma-independent Lord would be partial.

notes: Nyāya Sūtra side from memory (U11 owns the text); no teaching id created here.

question: Can the Lord be only the efficient cause of the world, as the Māheśvaras teach? (Brahma Sūtra 2.2.37ff, paśupati-adhikaraṇa)

sides.position: The Lord is the cause; the effect - vidyā, kalā, paśu - is eternal and depends on him; Rudra is the efficient cause, his Kalā the other cause (as Yāmuna reports).
arguments: The Lord produces, favours and conceals the effect in play (PABh on PS 1.9).
As a potter is only the efficient cause of a pot, a conscious ruler is only the efficient cause (their reasoning as reported by Vācaspati).

sides.position: Brahman is both the material and the efficient cause; the view of a Lord who is only ruler is non-Vedic and inconsistent (partiality, no possible relation, no support for ruling insentient matter, finitude or non-omniscience).
arguments: Patyur asāmañjasyāt (BS 2.2.37) and the following sūtras, as explained by Śaṅkara.

sides.position: The Paśupati doctrine is contrary to the Veda and internally inconsistent; its practices (insignia, skull-eating, corpse-ash) are non-Vedic.
arguments: Rāmānuja on the paśupati-adhikaraṇa, following Yāmuna.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the disagreement concerns whether the Lord is also the material cause of the world.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the Pāśupata analyses the world as eternal effect under a ruler (causal standpoint); Vedānta speaks of Brahman as the substance of all (substance standpoint).
No reconciliation: Vedānta treats the non-material-cause view as contrary to śruti.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Both Vedānta schools reject the Pāśupata view as non-Vedic; the Pāśupatas count Vedāntic and Sāṃkhya causes among the effects (PABh 5.46).

question: Is the Pāśupata (and wider Atimārga) teaching within or outside the Veda?

sides.position: The Pāśupata path is the best of all paths, the true path, others being bad paths; its scripture comes from Maheśvara through the teachers; it uses the Vedic brahma-mantras and is for brahmins; only from the Pañcārtha comes true ascertainment of reality.
arguments: PS 4.16-18; PABh on PS 1.1 (āgama); SDS ch. 6 ('pañcārthād anyato nāsti yathāvat tattvaniścayaḥ').

sides.position: The Vedic Pāśupata vow of the Atharvaśiras is to be followed; the Pāśupata, Soma, Lākula, Vāma and Bhairava scriptures are non-Vedic and were taught for delusion.
arguments: Kūrma P. 2.37.140-146; 1.15.111-113; Śiva P. 7.1.33 (the śrauta Pāśupata vow).

sides.position: All four Māheśvara groups are outside the Veda: they contradict the Vedic Brahman as material and efficient cause and devise āśramas outside the Vedic order.
arguments: Yāmuna, Āgamaprāmāṇya; Rāmānuja, Śrībhāṣya 2.2.35ff.

sides.position: Pāśupata is one of five systems of knowledge (with Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pañcarātra and the Vedas), taught by Śiva Śrīkaṇṭha; Nārāyaṇa is the foundation in all.
arguments: Mahābhārata 12.337.59-64 (Nārāyaṇīya).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Pāśupatas claim the highest path; Purāṇic and Vaiṣṇava critics place the Pāśupata scriptures outside the Veda.
candidate_readings: P3-path: the Nārāyaṇīya's own stance - several systems for different temperaments with one foundation.
P4-stage: the Pāśupata presents itself as a state beyond the āśramas for qualified brahmins (atyāśrama).
No reconciliation: the Kūrma Purāṇa and Yāmuna explicitly deny Vedic authority to these scriptures.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Kūrma Purāṇa and Yāmuna reject any inclusive reading; the Pāśupata Sūtra calls all other paths bad paths.

question: Is the Atimārga's liberation final, or a lower level beneath Śiva?

sides.position: By this rule the brahmin reaches Rudra's proximity and does not return; the end of suffering by the Lord's grace is final, certain and absolute.
arguments: PS 4.19-20; PS 5.35-40; PABh on PS 2.15-18 (final, non-returning proximity).

sides.position: Pāśupatas reach the level of Īśvara (Aiśvara pada) and skull-observers the Dhruva; they are not re-created, yet all that the Atimārga attains is attained with ease in Śiva-knowledge, which is higher.

reconciliation.explanation: Both sides agree the Atimārga follower is not reborn; the Mantramārga's own graded scheme reads that goal as a high but not highest stage.
reconciliation.detail: This records the Mantramārga's inclusivist ranking as a stage-reading; it does not claim that the Pāśupata goal is lower, only that one tradition so ranks it.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Pāśupata tradition would reject being ranked below another path: its sūtra calls all other paths bad paths (PS 4.16-18) and its end of suffering final.

question: Who may be initiated into the Atimārga observances: brahmin men only, or anyone?

sides.position: Only brahmin men: the disciple is a tested brahmin; 'no brahmin returns' restricts the path to brahmins; the practitioner must not speak with women or śūdras.
arguments: PABh on PS 1.1 and 4.20; PS 1.12-17.

sides.position: As reported by opponents: by entry into initiation one becomes a brahmin at once, and by the Kāpāla vow a man becomes an ascetic.
arguments: Yāmuna, Āgamaprāmāṇya (opponent's report).

sides.position: Jain doxographers report that the Śaiva bharaṭas take the vow without regard to varṇa, and that even a slave who keeps the Śaiva initiation for twelve years attains nirvāṇa (report of the Naiyāyika-Śaivas' saying).
arguments: Guṇaratna; Rājaśekhara.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Pāśupata restricts eligibility by birth; other Śaiva groups (as reported) do not.
candidate_readings: P4-stage (adhikāra): each school defines qualification differently - which is itself the point at issue.
Different Śaiva orders at different periods may simply have differed in rule.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Kauṇḍinya's restriction to brahmins is explicit; a reconciliation must not erase it.

question: At liberation, are the Lord's qualities transferred to, possessed by or produced in the soul - or is the soul's own Śiva-nature manifested?

sides.position: The liberated gains the Lord's qualities: powers of knowing and acting, the marks of perfection, union with Rudra ('attainment of the qualities' as the gain of the fifth stage).
arguments: PS 1.21-38; PABh on PS 5.29 ('guṇāvāpti'); SDS ch. 6.

sides.position: Liberation is the manifestation of the soul's own Śiva-nature, not the transfer, possession or production of qualities; it comes through initiation, the Lord's act.
arguments: Rāmakaṇṭha, Kiraṇavṛtti ch. 1.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Siddhānta explicitly rejects accounts in which the Lord's qualities come to the soul from outside.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: described from the Lord's giving (Pāśupata) or from the soul's latent nature (Siddhānta).
No reconciliation: the Siddhānta's rejection is explicit.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Rāmakaṇṭha denies saṅkrānti, āveśa and samutpatti by name; which rival schools held them is not stated in the passage.

question: Is liberation only the cessation of suffering, or also the attainment of lordship?

sides.position: It is twofold: cessation and lordship; elsewhere liberation is only cessation or isolation, but even those liberated by Sāṃkhya-Yoga remain paśus.
arguments: SDS ch. 6; PABh on PS 1.1 and 5.46.

sides.position: Liberation is isolation (kaivalya) of the person from matter (position as characterised by the Pāśupatas; the Sāṃkhya unit holds the texts).
Liberation (apavarga) is absolute release from pain; Yāmuna even reports the Pāśupatas' end of suffering in these terms, as the destruction of the soul's special qualities.
arguments: Yāmuna's report.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: the Pāśupatas insist their goal exceeds cessation and isolation.
candidate_readings: P2-standpoint: the impersonal aspect (cessation) is common ground; the personal aspect (lordship) is the Pāśupata's distinctive claim.
No reconciliation: the Pāśupatas deny that the Sāṃkhya-liberated are free.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Kauṇḍinya calls even the Sāṃkhya-Yoga liberated paśus.

question: Is the Kāpālika way (skull vow, insignia, liquor, consort, Bhairava rites) a path to liberation?

sides.position: As reported: knowing and wearing the insignia, meditation on the self in the yoni, and the Lord's own path of liquor and the beloved lead to release (voiced only through opponents and satirists).
arguments: Āgamaprāmāṇya (report); Mattavilāsa v. 7 (satire); Prabodhacandrodaya act 3 (hostile).

sides.position: Release comes only from knowing Brahman (Vāsudeva); these practices are outside the Veda.
arguments: Yāmuna: 'tam eva viditvā atimṛtyum eti...'.

sides.position: The Kāpālikas are deluded opponents defeated by Śaṅkara (hagiography) and by Viveka (allegorical drama).
arguments: Śaṅkaradigvijaya cantos 11, 15; Prabodhacandrodaya act 3.

historical_debates.name: Śaṅkara and the Kāpālikas (Ugrabhairava at Śrīśaila; Krakaca at Ujjayinī)
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Advaita hagiography: the Kāpālikas are defeated; no Kāpālika account survives.

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled - and not fairly reconcilable while the Kāpālika side survives only in opponents' words.
candidate_readings: Await any first-hand Kāpālika/Somasiddhānta text before assessing.
P6-upaya: the skull vow as penance modelled on the Lord's own act (Kūrma P. 2.31) - a reading the critics do not accept.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The critics deny any validity; no Kāpālika voice is available.
